title: Peace three times: om shanti
hookLine: a student gives back all he learned, partridges peck it up, and their school asks for peace
carry: shanti three times: within, around, beyond
tomorrow: what did Krishna say about results you can't control?

cards: The Vishnu Purana tells how one school got its strange name. A teacher, Vaishampayana, and his proud student, Yajnavalkya, fall out. The angry teacher says: then give back everything you learned from me.
And Yajnavalkya does. He brings up the verses he had learned, right there. The other students take the form of partridges, tittiri, and peck them up.
That, the story says, is why their branch of the Veda is called Taittiriya: the partridge school.

teach.b: Now hear the peace chant that opens the second part of the Taittiriya Upanishad, still chanted before study across India.

teach.h: MAY WE NOT HATE EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Teacher and student say it together: may God protect us both, may God nourish us both, may we work together with strength, may our study shine, and may we not hate each other.

Some teachers hear the story in that line: a school born of a quarrel between teacher and student asks, every time it begins, not to quarrel. Then comes om, shantih, shantih, shantih. Why three times?
The traditional explanation is that suffering comes from three directions, so peace is asked three times. Adhyatmika: trouble from within, your own body and mind.
Adhibhautika: trouble from other beings, the people and creatures around you. Adhidaivika: trouble from beyond anyone's control, storm and fate and the powers above.
Peace within, peace around, peace from beyond. That's why so many Hindu prayers, pujas and readings close this way. And listen to how it ends.

Shantih is written with a visarga, an h with a dot under it; in Devanagari, two small dots like a colon. It's a release of breath after the vowel, and reciters often let it carry a faint echo: shanti-hi.
Some keep it faint, some let it ring. Om closes with the other mark, anusvara, a hum through the nose.
So the chant ends the way it asks: the word is over, and the peace is still breathing out.

how: Teachers and students across India chant saha nāvavatu before study, and countless pujas, readings and gatherings close with om shantih shantih shantih, traditionally explained as peace from three sources of trouble; reciters let the final visarga breathe out softly.

o: a mark that makes a vowel twice as long
a hum through the nose after a vowel
a soft breath released after a vowel

games.q: peace three times — tap the pairs.
p: trouble from within: body and mind

s: in the story, the partridges are the other students, pecking up what Yajnavalkya gave back
the Vishnu Purana says that is how the Taittiriya, the partridge school, got its name.
shanti is said three times just to fit the rhythm
the traditional explanation: peace from three sources of trouble, within, around and beyond.
the hi heard at the end of shantih is added by the singer
it's written: the visarga, a breath after the vowel, often echoing it.

games.q: a teacher and a student sit down to study together. what does their peace chant ask, just before the three shantis?
o: that the student come first in the class.
that they not hate each other.
games.why: may we not hate each other, then peace three times. some teachers hear the partridge school remembering its own quarrel.

practice: If you chant, say om and let the m hum until the breath runs out. Then say shantih three times, slowly, one on each out-breath, letting the visarga carry its soft echo.
With the first, think of your own body and mind; with the second, the people and creatures near you; with the third, everything no one controls.
If you would rather not chant, say the word peace three times inwardly, with the same three in mind.

wordCard.voice: Visarga. The breath after the vowel, as in shantiḥ, said shanti-hi: the peace still breathing out.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: śāntiḥ, peace. The two dots at the end are the visarga.
